newsitem.title: USA: Round-the-world U.S. balloonist alters route.
newsitem.headline: Round-the-world U.S. balloonist alters route.

text.p: American Steve Fossett, an eighth of the way along in his bid to circle the world in a balloon, was negotiating with the Libyan government on Wednesday for permisson to cross that country.

His Chicago-based expedition said the 52-year-old adventurer was more than 600 miles (1,000 km) east-southeast of Bermuda at 4:30 p.m. EST (2130 GMT) and was trying to clear the way for a passage over North Africa this weekend.
He was forced to take a more southerly path than originally planned since he could not win permission from Russia for a northern trans-European route.
"There are significant concerns about Libya," the mission's chief spokesman, Bo Kemper, told Reuters. "The United States has no formal diplomatic relations with Libya. We are trying to work it out."

Kemper said the Colorado-based commodities broker had travelled more than 2,200 miles (3,500 km) since lifting off from St. Louis on Monday night -- an eighth of the way around the globe in his bid to achieve one of manned flight's oldest goals.
Kemper said an earlier projection that Fossett might also have to cross over Iraq had been revised and that mission organisers did not currently foresee that happening.
The expedition said a number of minor problems, including language barriers affecting Fossett and flight controllers, made passage over Russia impossible.
Fossett was at 22,000 feet (6,700 metres) trying to catch winds that would push his craft along a more southerly route.
He hoped to head to Gibraltar, across Morocco, Algeria, Libya, Egypt, Iran, Afghanistan, Pakistan, China, Mongolia, China again, perhaps Korea and then out across the Pacific, the expedition said.
Kemper said Fossett was eating "meals ready to eat" -- prepared food used by the U.S. military -- and taking antacids to counteract their impact on his stomach.

He was able to sleep for periods of time in his unpressurized, six and one-half feet (two meters) long by four feet (1.3 metre) wide yellow capsule, which is equipped with an alarm to rouse him should the balloon suddenly change altitude. The enclosed gondola is five and one-half feet high (1.7 metres).
"Things are going quite well," Kemper said.
The new route will not necessarily add more time to Fossett's attempt to be the first to circle the globe in a balloon nonstop, the expedition said. The trip could take up to 18 days.
Fossett is at the mercy of the Northern Hemisphere winter winds. He has no true directional control other than to change altitude to catch winds blowing in varying directions.

His origial route was to have taken him from Britain over Western Europe, Russia, Kazakhstan and China. After crossing southern Japan he would have bridged the Pacific northeast to Washington state and land somewhere east of St. Louis.
Internet users may follow the progress of his trip at http://www.luc.edu/solo. The site includes Fossett's latest transmissions from the balloon and offers a chance to ask him questions.

Fossett, who made a fortune in the Chicago futures markets, is financing the trip himself with scientific backing from Loyola University of Chicago, where his control centre is based. He made a similar attempt one year ago but crashed in Canada on the second day.

Two rival expeditions failed in the past week. A Swiss-Belgian team of Bertrand Piccard and Wim Verstraeten went down in the Mediterranean on Sunday six hours after taking off from the Swiss Alps, and British tycoon Richard Branson and two crew members brought their Virgin Global Challenger balloon down in Algeria last Wednesday less than 24 hours after taking off from Morocco.
In 1995 Fossett set a world distance record for a solo balloon flight when he flew from South Korea to Canada in 20 days and nine hours.
